primer.intro: A binary search tree is a binary tree with one promise added: at every node, everything in the left subtree is smaller than the node's value and everything in the right subtree is larger. The promise covers whole subtrees, all the way down - and that global reach is what beginners miss first. From one invariant, everything else falls out: searching walks a single root-to-leaf path, discarding an entire subtree per step; the minimum is the leftmost node and the maximum the rightmost; and the inorder traversal of the previous topic prints the values in sorted ascending order. A BST is best understood as binary search, frozen into pointers.
whenToUse: A changing set needs fast membership, insertion and ordered queries at once.
Floor and ceil questions: the nearest stored values on either side of a target.
The kth smallest or largest of a dynamic set - inorder plus a counter.
Sorted output must be produced from tree-shaped data: one inorder walk.
primer.mentalModel: Think in ranges. The root may hold anything; stepping left caps the allowed values from above, stepping right raises the floor. Every node therefore lives inside an interval narrowed by each ancestor turn, and validating a BST means passing that interval down - a node checked only against its own children can still break the promise against a great-grandparent. Searching rides the same ranges: compare, discard the impossible side, step. Floor and ceil fall out of the search path for free - walking right past a smaller value makes it the floor candidate, walking left past a larger value makes it the ceil candidate, and the last candidates standing when the walk ends are the answers.
mistakes: Validating by comparing each node with just its children - the invariant binds whole subtrees, so pass ranges down.
Assuming the height is log n; insert sorted data and the tree is a chain with linear operations.
Recursing into an insert and discarding the returned subtree - the new node is built and then lost.

example.title: Search as a guided walk
example.explain: Each comparison discards one whole subtree: too big, go left; too small, go right. The loop touches one node per level, so the cost is the height - about log n on a balanced tree, n on a chain. No recursion is needed because nothing happens on the way back up; search is the rare tree routine that is more natural as a loop. Insert is this same walk that remembers the last node and hangs the new value off the side the walk fell from.

primer.practice: Open Practice with Search in BST; the walk you write there is the skeleton of floor, ceil, insert and the validity check.

sections.title: An invariant about ranges
sections.text: The sorting power and the classic bug both live in the same fact: the promise is global. To validate, hand every node an interval. The root gets an unbounded one; a left child inherits its parent's interval with the ceiling lowered to the parent's value; a right child gets the floor raised. A tree is a BST exactly when every node sits inside its inherited interval. The tempting shortcut - check each node against its immediate children - accepts trees where a deep right-side value sneaks above an old ceiling. And the one-line certificate: a tree is a BST exactly when its inorder traversal comes out strictly increasing.

check.prompt: A tree's inorder traversal prints 2 5 7 8 12 14 - strictly increasing. What does that certify?

options.text: The tree is balanced
options.explain: A sorted chain prints the same sequence; shape stays unknown.

options.text: Only that the root is between 2 and 14
options.explain: True but weak - the full certificate covers every node.

options.text: Nothing without also checking each node's children
options.explain: The inorder test is complete on its own; no second pass is needed.

options.text: The tree is a valid BST
options.explain: Inorder strictly increasing and being a BST are the same condition.

reveal.solution: Inorder prints left subtree, node, right subtree. If the sequence is strictly increasing, then at every node everything printed before it - its entire left subtree - is smaller, and everything after - its right subtree - is larger. That is precisely the BST promise at every node, so the sorted sequence is a complete certificate. Shape, balance and height remain unknown.

sections.title: The search path pays twice
sections.text: Most BST tasks are one walk down with a notebook. Floor of x: walk the search path; every time you step right past a value smaller than or equal to x, write it down; the last note is the floor. Ceil mirrors it on left steps. Insert: walk until the pointer falls off, then hang the new node on the side you fell from - and when writing it recursively, assign the recursive result back to the child link, or the new node is created and garbage-collected in the same breath. Kth smallest: run inorder with a live counter and stop the walk the moment the counter hits k; kth largest is the same walk mirrored right-to-left.

quiz.prompt: A changing set of numbers needs membership checks and ordered listing. Which structure fits?

options.text: An unsorted list
options.explain: Both operations degrade to full scans.

options.text: A binary search tree - height-cost search plus a sorted inorder walk
options.explain: One structure answers both: the walk discards a subtree per step, inorder lists sorted.

options.text: A sorted array
options.explain: Search is fast, but every insertion shifts elements - linear per change.

options.text: A hash table
options.explain: Membership is fast, but ordered listing needs a full sort every time.

quiz.prompt: Find the kth smallest value in a BST. Which plan uses the structure best?

options.text: Level order, counting served nodes
options.explain: Floor order has nothing to do with value order.

options.text: Repeatedly delete the minimum k times
options.explain: Destroys the tree to read from it.

options.text: Inorder walk with a live counter, stopping the moment it reaches k
options.explain: Inorder emits sorted order, so the kth visit is the answer - no array needed.

options.text: Copy all values out and sort them
options.explain: The tree is already sorted in its bones; sorting again wastes n log n.

quiz.prompt: Floor and ceil of x in a BST - the nearest stored values around it. How are they found?

options.text: Walk the search path, noting candidates at each turn; the last notes win
options.explain: Right steps update the floor, left steps the ceil - one walk, both answers.

options.text: Inorder the whole tree into an array, then scan
options.explain: Correct but linear; the path walk costs only the height.

options.text: Check the root's two children
options.explain: The neighbours of x can sit many levels deep on the path.

options.text: Find the minimum and maximum
options.explain: Those are the global extremes, unrelated to x's neighbourhood.

quiz.prompt: Validate that a tree is a genuine BST. Which check is sound?

options.text: Pass an allowed interval down; left narrows the top, right raises the bottom
options.explain: The promise binds whole subtrees, and intervals carry it to every depth.

options.text: Compare every node with its two children
options.explain: A deep value can violate a distant ancestor while all local pairs look fine.

options.text: Check that the minimum is in the leftmost node
options.explain: A necessary symptom, far from sufficient.

options.text: Check the root lies between its children
options.explain: One local comparison certifies almost nothing.

quiz.prompt: In the BST built from 8 5 12 2 7 -1 14, which nodes does the search for 7 visit, in order?

options.explain: Searches start at the root 8, nowhere else.
At 5 the walk turns right immediately; 2 is on the discarded side.
7 is smaller than 8 (go left), larger than 5 (go right), found.
7 is smaller than 8, so the whole right subtree is discarded.

quiz.prompt: Same BST (values 2 5 7 8 12 14). Floor and ceil of 6?

options.text: 2 and 14
options.explain: Those are the global min and max, blind to the target.

options.text: 5 and 8
options.explain: 7 stands between 6 and 8 and is the tighter ceiling.

options.text: 5 and 7
options.explain: 5 is the largest stored value at most 6; 7 the smallest at least 6.

options.text: 7 and 5
options.explain: Floor sits below the target, ceil above - these are swapped.

quiz.prompt: Insert 9 into the BST holding 2 5 7 8 12 14, then walk inorder. What prints?

options.explain: Then it would no longer be sorted - inorder on a BST cannot print this.
9 is no root; it hangs off 12's left as a leaf.
The insert must actually attach the node - this is the lost-link symptom.
Inorder is always sorted, and 9 slots between 8 and 12.

quiz.prompt: What do search and insert cost in a BST of n nodes?

options.text: Proportional to the height: about log n balanced, n on a chain
options.explain: One node per level; the shape sets the bill.

options.text: Always log n
options.explain: Only balanced shapes earn the logarithm; sorted inserts build a chain.

options.text: Always constant
options.explain: The walk visits one node per level - at least one level per step of depth.

options.text: Always linear
options.explain: Linear is the chain's worst case, beaten badly by any bushy shape.

quiz.prompt: Kth smallest via inorder-with-counter, stopping at k. The cost?

options.text: About the height plus k visits
options.explain: The walk descends to the minimum, then emits k values and stops.

options.text: Always the full n
options.explain: Early stopping is the point - nothing after the kth visit runs.

options.text: k log n
options.explain: Successive inorder visits are amortized constant, with one descent up front.

options.text: Constant
options.explain: Reaching the minimum alone already costs the height.

quiz.prompt: This validator accepts a tree where 9 sits deep in the left subtree of root 8. What is the bug?

options.text: The equality test is missing on the left side
options.explain: Duplicates matter too, but the accepted 9 is a range violation, deeper than that.

options.text: The recursion visits children twice
options.explain: Each child is visited once per side; the flaw is what is compared.

options.text: Only parent-child pairs are checked; the promise binds whole subtrees - pass ranges down
options.explain: The 9 is fine against its own parent but violates the root's ceiling of 8.

options.text: The null checks are in the way
options.explain: The guards are correct; the comparison scope is what falls short.

quiz.prompt: After this insert the tree looks unchanged. What is the bug?

options.text: The comparison direction is flipped
options.explain: Larger values going right is the convention, and it is honoured here.

options.text: The base case builds the node wrongly
options.explain: The node literal is fine; it is just unreachable from the tree.

options.text: return node is in the way
options.explain: Returning the subtree root is exactly right - once the links are reassigned.

options.text: The recursive result is thrown away - assign node.right or node.left to it
options.explain: The new leaf is built and instantly lost; the parent's link still points at null.

quiz.prompt: Which target most deserves a dedicated test for a floor-and-ceil routine?

options.text: A large balanced tree
options.explain: Size stresses performance; the empty-side answer stresses correctness.

options.text: A target between two deep leaves
options.explain: Worth having, but the unwritten-candidate path breaks real code more often.

options.text: A target below the minimum - the floor must come back empty, ceil the minimum
options.explain: One candidate side stays unwritten; the empty answer path must work.

options.text: A target equal to the root
options.explain: Easy case: both answers are the root itself.
